Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette: When the night sky over Houston darkened, Zayn, a twenty‑six‑year‑old veterinarian who works long shifts at the city animal clinic, was walking home after a late evening of grooming and administering injections. A shadowy figure stepped out from behind a parked van, demanded a wallet, and brandished a small knife. In the heat of the moment Zayn tried to comply, handing over the wallet without protest, then stepped back to the curb as the attacker ran into the night. The abrupt loss of safety, the cold steel of the weapon, and the scream that followed were seared into Zayn’s memory. In the weeks that followed, Zayn’s sense of well‑being eroded. He no longer felt the same joy in a day’s work; he described a hollow feeling, saying, “I used to be happy, but now I am always miserable.” He began to distrust anyone who offered help, believing that he could not rely on others, and he became convinced that a danger could strike at any moment. These negative appraisals pushed Zayn into a set of coping habits: he would tell himself the robbery was not real or that it wasn’t that bad—magical thinking that minimized the event—while also becoming overly compliant whenever he sensed threat, a fawn response that kept him safe but prevented him from confronting the pain. He started to avoid going out, refusing even to leave the clinic after closing hours. When an ordinary sound—a distant siren or the clatter of a bicycle—reaches his ears, Zayn’s mind abruptly flashes back to the robbery. The memory intrudes without warning, and the scent of gun oil or the metallic tang of a street at dusk can bring the full terror rushing back. When he tries to explain what happened, he finds himself losing the thread and unable to finish the story. Each time this memory surfaces, Zayn instinctively falls back into his magical thinking, trying to convince himself the event never truly happened. The memory also triggers his threat monitoring: he checks behind him, scans the street, and feels an unrelenting alert at home, as if the house itself could be invaded. The ongoing threat vigilance keeps Zayn in a constant state of hyper‑alertness. Every time he hears a rumble of a truck or sees a flicker of movement, he instinctively adopts the same fawn response, staying compliant with anyone who might look hostile. This behavior reinforces the memory of the robbery, as each encounter with perceived danger feels eerily familiar. Moreover, his constant scanning amplifies his negative appraisal that he cannot rely on anyone, solidifying the belief that he must remain on guard at all times. Zayn’s maladaptive strategies now sustain the loop. When he declines to assist a client or chooses to leave the clinic early, he feels a fleeting sense of safety, but the memory of the robbery resurfaces with sharper clarity. His avoidance of public spaces has isolated him from friends and from his partner, who feels increasingly abandoned and frustrated. Each time Zayn stays inside, his perception of safety heightens only to collapse when he hears a noise outside, making the threat feel all the more real. The fawn response keeps him from confronting these patterns, and the magical thinking dulls his awareness of the cycle’s existence. The culmination of these intertwined processes has pushed Zayn to the point of exhaustion. He has missed appointments, his clinic’s client load has dropped, and his partner’s patience has worn thin. Sleep eludes him, and each night the memory returns, punctuated by the familiar scent of fear. The constant threat monitoring has left him emotionally drained. Finally, the accumulation of these stresses prompted Zayn to seek therapy, hoping to reclaim the happiness that once colored his days and to learn whether he could trust others again without feeling perpetually on guard.
